nodes.name: Basic arrangement of categories A, B, C with functors alpha, beta
nodes.statement: \begin{tikzcd} \mathcal{A} \arrow[rd, "\alpha"'] & & \mathcal{B} \arrow[ld, "\beta"] \\ & \calC & \end{tikzcd}
nodes.statement_short: Two functors $\alpha:\mathcal{A}\to\calC$ and $\beta:\mathcal{B}\to\calC$ into a common category.
nodes.label: eqn:abc

nodes.name: Comma category
nodes.statement: The comma category $\Comma{\alpha}{\beta}$ built from this arrangement has as objects \[ ob\paran{\Comma{\alpha}{\beta}} := \SetDef{ \paran{ a, b, \phi } }{ a\in ob(\calA), \, b\in ob(\calB), \, \phi \in \Hom_{\calC} \paran{ \alpha a ; \beta b } } , \] and the morphisms comprise of pairs $\SetDef{ (f,g) }{ f\in \Hom(D),\, g\in \Hom(E) }$ such that the following commutation holds : \[\begin{tikzcd} \blue{ (a,\phi,b) } \arrow{r}{ (f,g) } & \akashi{ (a',\phi',b') } \end{tikzcd} \,\Leftrightarrow \, \begin{tikzcd} a \arrow{d}{f} \\ a' \end{tikzcd}, \begin{tikzcd} b \arrow{d}{g} \\ b' \end{tikzcd}, \mbox{ s.t. } \begin{tikzcd} \blue{ \alpha a } \arrow{r}{\alpha f} \arrow[blue]{d}{\phi} & \akashi{ \alpha a' } \arrow[Akashi]{d}{\phi'} \\ \blue{ \beta b } \arrow{r}{\beta g} & \akashi{ \beta b' } \end{tikzcd}\]
nodes.statement_short: Objects of the comma category are triples $(a,b,\phi:\alpha a\to\beta b)$; morphisms are pairs $(f,g)$ making the square commute.

nodes.name: Forgetful functors of a comma category
nodes.statement: Comma categories contain as sub-structures, the original categories $\calA, \calB$, via the \emph{forgetful} functors \[\begin{tikzcd} \calA & \Comma{\alpha}{\beta} \arrow{l}[swap]{\Forget_1} \arrow{r}{\Forget_2} & \calB \end{tikzcd}\] whose action on morphisms in $\Comma{\alpha}{\beta}$ can be described as \[ \begin{tikzcd} a \arrow{d}{f} \\ a' \end{tikzcd} \begin{tikzcd} {} & & {} \arrow[ll, "\Forget_1"'] \end{tikzcd} \begin{tikzcd} \blue{ \alpha a } \arrow{r}{\alpha f} \arrow[blue]{d}{\phi} & \akashi{ \alpha a' } \arrow[Akashi]{d}{\phi'} \\ \blue{ \beta b } \arrow{r}{\beta g} & \akashi{ \beta b' } \end{tikzcd} \begin{tikzcd} {} \arrow[rr, "\Forget_2"] & & {} \end{tikzcd} \begin{tikzcd} b \arrow{d}{g} \\ b' \end{tikzcd} \]
nodes.statement_short: The two forgetful functors from $\Comma{\alpha}{\beta}$ to $\calA$ and $\calB$, projecting objects and morphisms.

nodes.name: Dynamical systems with measurements as a comma category
nodes.statement: \cite{DasSuda2024recon} Suppose $\calT$ is a semigroup, then it is representable as a 1-object category. Let $\Topo$ be the category of topological spaces and continuous maps. Then the class of topological dynamics is the functor category $\Functor{\calT}{\Topo}$. Now let $\EucCat$ be the subgroup of $\Topo$ comprised only of Euclidean spaces. Then the following arrangement is of the nature of \eqref{eqn:abc} : \[\begin{tikzcd} \Functor{\calT}{\Topo} \arrow[bend right = 20]{dr}[swap]{\dom} & & \EucCat \arrow[bend left = 20]{dl}{\subset} \\ & \Topo \end{tikzcd}\] leads to a comma category. The domain functor $\dom$ above assigns to every dynamical system its domain. A typical object in this category is a dynamical systems $(\Omega, \Phi^t)$ along with a measurement $\phi : \Omega\to \real^d$ : \[\begin{tikzcd} \Omega \arrow{r}{\Phi^t} & \Omega \arrow{r}{\phi} & \real^{d} \end{tikzcd}\] A typical morphism in this comma category is a change of variables $h:\Omega\to \Omega'$ that leads to the following joint commutation : \[\begin{tikzcd} [row sep = large] \Omega \arrow{d}[swap]{h} \arrow[blue]{r}{\Phi^t} & \Omega \arrow{d}[swap]{h} \arrow[blue]{r}{\phi} & \real^{d} \arrow{d}[swap]{\iota A} \\ \Omega' \arrow[Holud]{r}{\Phi'^t} & \Omega' \arrow[Holud]{r}{\phi'} & \real^{d'} \end{tikzcd} , \quad \forall t\in \calT .\]
nodes.statement_short: Topological dynamical systems with Euclidean measurements form a comma category; morphisms are compatible changes of variables.
nodes.label: ex:dyn_obs

nodes.name: Affine maps between finite dimensional spaces as a comma category
nodes.statement: Let $\AffineCat$ be the category of vector spaces and affine maps, and $\FinVect$ be the category of finite dimensional vector spaces and linear maps. Then the following arrangement \[\begin{tikzcd} \FinVect \arrow[bend right = 20]{dr}[swap]{\subset} & & \FinVect \arrow[bend left = 20]{dl}{\subset} \\ & \AffineCat \end{tikzcd}\] leads to a comma category in which the objects are affine maps between finite dimensional vector spaces, and the morphisms are pairs of linear transformations that perform a change of variables. This category is the key to a generalized notion of nullity \cite{HSYprevalence1992}.
nodes.label: ex:Affine:1

nodes.name: One-point category $\star$
nodes.statement: Henceforth, we shall use the symbol $\star$ to denote the category with a single object with no non-trivial morphism.
differentia: with a single object with no non-trivial morphism

nodes.name: Object as a functor from the one-point category
nodes.statement: Take any category $\calX$, and an object $x$ in it. This object may be interpreted by a unique functor from $\star$ to $\calX$, which we shall also denote by $\star \xrightarrow{x} \calX$.

nodes.name: Left slice category
nodes.statement: Now set \[ \calB = \star, \, \calA = \calC = \calX, \, \beta = x, \, \alpha = \Id_{\calX} , \] in \eqref{eqn:abc}. The resulting comma category $\Comma{\Id_{\calX}}{x}$ is known as the left slice of $x$ in $\calX$, and will be denoted more briefly as $\Comma{\calX}{x}$. A typical morphism in this category is shown below \[\begin{tikzcd} y \arrow[r, "f", blue] \arrow[d, "\phi"'] & x \\ y' \arrow[ru, "f'"', Akashi] & \end{tikzcd}\] The objects are the morphisms shown in blue, and a morphism $\phi$ from $f$ to $f'$ is a morphism $\phi:y\to y'$ such that the above commutation holds.
nodes.statement_short: The left slice $\Comma{\calX}{x}$ is the comma category $\Comma{\Id_{\calX}}{x}$: arrows into $x$ with commuting triangles as morphisms.

nodes.name: Left slice of a topological space in Top
nodes.statement: Let $\calU$ be any topological space. Then its left slice $\Comma{\Topo}{\calU}$ in $\Topo$ is the category formed by the collection of all continuous maps into $\calU$.
nodes.label: ex:powset:1

nodes.name: Left slice in a power set is a power set
nodes.statement: Let $\calU$ be a set and $2^{\calU}$ be the power set of $\calU$. Thus $2^{\calU}$ is a preorder and a category. Then the left slice of any set $S\subset \calU$ in $2^{\calU}$ is the power set of $S$.
nodes.label: ex:powset:2

nodes.name: Subobject category as a left slice
nodes.statement: More generally, let $\calC$ be any category and $\calC_{mono}$ be the subcategory comprising only of monomorphisms. Then the left slice of any object $c$ of $\calC$ in $\calC_{mono}$ is the \emph{subobject category} of $c$.
nodes.label: ex:subob:1

nodes.name: Comma category over the second forgetful functor (L-shaped diagrams)
nodes.statement: Given the arrangement as in \eqref{eqn:abc} one has the following diagram : \[\begin{tikzcd} \Comma{\alpha}{\beta} \arrow[rd, "\Forget_2"'] & & \star \arrow[ld, "b"] \\ & \mathcal{B} & \end{tikzcd}\] where $b$ is an object of $\calB$ and $\star$ is the 1-point category. This arrangement creates the comma category $\Comma{ \Forget_2^{ \Comma{\alpha}{\beta} } }{ b} $, whose objects are \begin{equation} ob \paran{ \Comma{ \Forget_2^{ \Comma{\alpha}{\beta} } }{ b} } := \braces{ \begin{tikzcd} \alpha a' \arrow[d, "f"] \\ \beta b' \end{tikzcd}, \; \begin{tikzcd} b' \arrow[d, "g"] \\ b \end{tikzcd} } \end{equation} Every such object creates an L-shaped diagram : \[\begin{tikzcd} \alpha a' \arrow[d, "f"'] \\ \beta b' \arrow[r, "\beta g"] & \beta b' \end{tikzcd}\] This is a diagram within $\calC$ in which one arrow $f$ is drawn from $\calC$, while another $g$ is drawn from $\calB$.
nodes.statement_short: Composing the forgetful functor $\Forget_2$ with an object $b$ gives a comma category whose objects are L-shaped diagrams.
nodes.label: ex:abstract:1

nodes.name: Objects of the comma category of Forget_2 over b
nodes.statement: ob \paran{ \Comma{ \Forget_2^{ \Comma{\alpha}{\beta} } }{ b} } := \braces{ \begin{tikzcd} \alpha a' \arrow[d, "f"] \\ \beta b' \end{tikzcd}, \; \begin{tikzcd} b' \arrow[d, "g"] \\ b \end{tikzcd} }
nodes.label: eqn:eodpc9

nodes.name: Arrow category
nodes.statement: If we set \[ \calA = \calB = \calC = \calX, \, \alpha = \beta = \Id_{\calX} , \] in \eqref{eqn:abc}, then the resulting comma category $\Comma{\Id_{\calX}}{\Id_{\calX}}$ is called the arrow category of $\calX$, and is denoted by $\ArrowCat{\calX}$. The objects in this category are the arrows or morphisms in $\calX$. A morphism between two arrows $x \xrightarrow{f} x'$ and $y \xrightarrow{g} y'$ is a pair of morphisms $x \xrightarrow{\phi} y$ and $x' \xrightarrow{\phi'} y'$ such that the following commutation holds : \[\begin{tikzcd} x \arrow[r, "f"] \arrow[d, "\phi"'] & x' \arrow[d, "\phi'"] \\ y \arrow[r, "g"] & y' \end{tikzcd}\]
nodes.statement_short: The arrow category $\ArrowCat{\calX}=\Comma{\Id}{\Id}$: objects are arrows of $\calX$, morphisms are commuting squares.

nodes.name: Arrow category of Top: topological pairs
nodes.statement: The arrow category $\ArrowCat{\Topo}$ in $\Topo$ corresponds to the category of topological pairs.
nodes.label: ex:Topo:1

nodes.name: Arrow category of Vect: linear maps
nodes.statement: The arrow category $\ArrowCat{\VectCat}$ in $\VectCat$ corresponds to the category of linear maps, with linear change of variables serving as morphisms.
nodes.label: ex:Vect:1

nodes.name: Inclusion of power set into subspaces of a topological space
nodes.statement: Recall the notations in Examples \ref{ex:powset:1} and \ref{ex:powset:2}. Let $\calU$ be a topological space. Take $\calX$ to be the power set $2^{\calU}$ and $\calY$ to be the subcategory of $\Topo$ formed by all topological subspaces of $\calU$. Then one has an obvious inclusion $\iota : \calX \to \calY$ which satisfy all of Assumptions \ref{A:1}, \ref{A:3}, \ref{A:4} and \ref{A:5}. Note that the comma category $\Comma{\iota}{\iota}$ has the same objects as the arrow category $\ArrowCat{\calY}$, but a different collection of morphisms. Any object $F\in \ArrowCat{\calY}$ is a continuous map between topological spaces $F:X\to Y$.
nodes.statement_short: Inclusion of $2^{\calU}$ into subspaces of $\calU$ satisfies the standing assumptions; $\Comma{\iota}{\iota}$ vs the arrow category.
nodes.label: ex:powset:5

nodes.name: Assumption A:1 (complete categories, continuous injective-on-objects functor)
nodes.statement: There are complete categories $\calX$ and $\calY$, with initial objects $0_{\calX}$ and $0_{\calY}$ respectively, and there is a continuous functor $\iota : \calX \to \calY$ such that $0_{\calY} = \iota \paran{ 0_{\calX} }$, and $\iota$ is injective on objects.
nodes.statement_short: Complete $\calX,\calY$ with initial objects; $\iota$ continuous, preserves the initial object and is injective on objects.
nodes.label: A:1

nodes.name: Category of small categories $\CatCat$
nodes.statement: Let $\CatCat$ denote the category of small categories.

nodes.name: Category of left slices $\LSlice{\calX}$
nodes.statement: Let $\LSlice{ \calX }$ denote the full subcategory of $\CatCat$ generated by the slice categories \[ \Comma{\calX}{\Omega}, \quad \Omega \in ob(\calX) . \]

nodes.name: Image subcategory $\iota(\calX)$
nodes.statement: Let $\iota(\calX)$ denote the full subcategory of $\calY$ generated by objects of $\iota$.

nodes.name: Epimorphism (surjective morphism)
nodes.statement: Recall that a morphism $f$ in any category is said to be \emph{surjective} or equivalently, an \emph{epimorphism}, if for any composable morphisms $g,g'$, if $g'f = gf$, then $g=g'$.
differentia: for any composable morphisms $g,g'$, if $g'f = gf$, then $g=g'$

nodes.name: Monomorphism (injective morphism)
nodes.statement: Similarly, a morphism is said to be \emph{injective} or equivalently, a \emph{monomorphism}, if for any composable morphisms $g,g'$, if $fg' = fg$, then $g=g'$.
differentia: for any composable morphisms $g,g'$, if $fg' = fg$, then $g=g'$

nodes.name: Assumption A:3 (monomorphisms factor through the image of iota)
nodes.statement: For every monomorphism $f$ in $\calY$, there are morphisms $g$ in $\calY$ and $h$ in $\calY$ such that $f = (\iota h) g$.
nodes.label: A:3

nodes.name: Assumption A:4 (iota maps morphisms to monomorphisms)
nodes.statement: The image under $\iota$ of every morphism in $\calX$ is injective in $\calY$.
nodes.label: A:4

nodes.name: Assumption A:5 (mono plus epi implies iso)
nodes.statement: Any morphism in $\calY$ which is both surjective and injective is an isomorphism.
nodes.label: A:5

nodes.name: Categories satisfying Assumption A:5
nodes.statement: Assumption \ref{A:5} is satisfied in categories such as topoi \cite{Goldblatt2014topoi, Freyd1972topoi, Brook1975fin}. $\SetCat$, $\Topo$ are two prime examples of topoi. Another important category in which Assumption \ref{A:5} is satisfied is $\GroupCat$, the category of groups and homomorphisms.

nodes.name: Functor from comma arrows to left slices (Dyn)
nodes.statement: Let Assumptions \ref{A:1}, \ref{A:3}, \ref{A:4} and \ref{A:5} hold. Then there is a functor \[ \iota(\calX) \xrightarrow{\Dyn} \LSlice{ \calX } , \] which maps every object $\Omega\in \calX$ to the left slice $\Comma{\calX}{\Omega}$. It maps an arrow $\iota \Omega \xrightarrow{F} \iota \Omega'$ into a functor $$\Comma{\calX}{\Omega} \xrightarrow{\tau_F} \Comma{\calX}{\Omega'}$$ such that for every $A \xrightarrow{a} \Omega \in \Comma{\calX}{\Omega}$, $\tau_F(a)$ creates a commutation square \begin{equation} \begin{tikzcd} \iota A \arrow[d, "\iota a"'] \\ \iota \Omega \arrow[r, "F"'] & \iota \Omega' \end{tikzcd} \imply \begin{tikzcd} \iota A \arrow[d, "\iota a"'] \arrow[r, "\tau_F(a)", Shobuj] & \iota B \arrow[d, "\iota b", Shobuj] \\ \iota \Omega \arrow[r, "F"'] & \iota \Omega' \end{tikzcd} \end{equation} for some $B \xrightarrow{b} \Omega \in \Comma{\calX}{\Omega'}$. Moreover, this square is universal in the sense that for any slice-object $b':B'\to \Omega'$ and any morphism $f:\iota A \to \iota B'$, if the blue commutation square shown below holds \begin{equation} \forall \begin{tikzcd} \end{tikzcd} \begin{tikzcd} & & \iota B' \arrow[ldd, "\iota b'", bend left=49, Akashi] \\ \iota A \arrow[d, "\iota a"', Akashi] \arrow[r, "\tau_F(a)", Shobuj] \arrow[rru, "f", bend left, Akashi] & \iota B \arrow[d, "\iota b", Shobuj] \arrow[ur, "\exists!\phi"', Holud] & \\ \iota \Omega \arrow[r, "F"', Akashi] & \iota \Omega' & \end{tikzcd} , \end{equation} then there is a unique morphism $\phi$ which factors the outer commutation loop into the inner commutation loop.
assumptions: Let Assumptions \ref{A:1}, \ref{A:3}, \ref{A:4} and \ref{A:5} hold.
conclusions: there is a functor \[ \iota(\calX) \xrightarrow{\Dyn} \LSlice{ \calX } , \] which maps every object $\Omega\in \calX$ to the left slice $\Comma{\calX}{\Omega}$
this square is universal
nodes.statement_short: Arrows $F:\iota\Omega\to\iota\Omega'$ in $\calY$ induce functors $\tau_F$ between left slices of $\calX$, functorially, via universal commuting squares.
nodes.label: thm:0

nodes.name: Induced maps between power sets from continuous maps
nodes.statement: Recall the notations in Example \ref{ex:powset:5}. Any object $F\in \Comma{\iota}{\iota}$ is a continuous map between topological spaces $F:X\to Y$. Then $\tau_F$ can be interpreted to be the induced map from the power set $\Comma{\iota}{X}$ of $X$, into the power set $\Comma{\iota}{Y}$ of $Y$. The correspondence between $F$ and $\tau_F$ is itself functorial. Overall, we have a functor $\Dyn : \Comma{\iota}{\iota} \to \LSlice{ 2^{\calU} }$. Note that $\LSlice{ 2^{\calU} }$ is the category in which each object is a power set of some $S\subset \calU$, and morphisms are inclusion preserving maps between these power sets.
nodes.statement_short: A continuous map $F:X\to Y$ induces the image map between power sets, giving a functor $\Dyn$ into $\LSlice{2^{\calU}}$.
nodes.label: ex:powset:3

nodes.name: Monomorphism subcategory of a complete category is complete
nodes.statement: Given any complete category $\calC$, the subcategory $\calC_{mono}$ formed by monomorphisms is complete, and has the same initial object as $\calC$.
assumptions: Given any complete category $\calC$
conclusions: the subcategory $\calC_{mono}$ formed by monomorphisms is complete
has the same initial object as $\calC$
nodes.label: lem:di0l

nodes.name: Functor from a category to its subobject categories
nodes.statement: Suppose $\calC$ is a complete category in which every morphism which is both a monormorphism and epimorphism is an isomorphism. Then : \begin{enumerate} [(i)] \item The inclusion $\iota : \calC_{mono} \to \calC$ satisfies Assumptions \ref{A:1}, \ref{A:3}, \ref{A:4} and \ref{A:5}. \item There is a functor $\Dyn$ from $\calC$ into the full subcategory of $\CatCat$ spanned by the sub-object categories of $\calC$. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: $\calC$ is a complete category in which every morphism which is both a monormorphism and epimorphism is an isomorphism
conclusions: The inclusion $\iota : \calC_{mono} \to \calC$ satisfies Assumptions \ref{A:1}, \ref{A:3}, \ref{A:4} and \ref{A:5}.
There is a functor $\Dyn$ from $\calC$ into the full subcategory of $\CatCat$ spanned by the sub-object categories of $\calC$.
nodes.statement_short: In a complete balanced category, $\calC_{mono}\subset\calC$ satisfies the assumptions, giving a functor $\Dyn$ to subobject categories.
nodes.label: corr:5

nodes.name: Linear maps induce maps between subspaces
nodes.statement: Continuing the discussion in Example \ref{ex:Vect:1}, any linear map $A: U\to V$ between vector spaces induces a mapping between the subspaces of $U$ and $V$ respectively. This correspondence is a functor from $\VectCat$ to the category of collections of vector subspaces.
nodes.label: ex:Vect:2

nodes.name: Affine maps and subspaces
nodes.statement: Take $\calX = \VectCat_{mono}$ and $\calY = \AffineCat$. The initial objects $0_\calX$ into $0_{\calY}$ are both the zero-dimensional vector space. Note that there is an inclusion functor $\iota : \calX \to \calY$ which maps $0_\calX$ into $0_{\calY}$. Thus according to Theorem \ref{thm:0} any affine map is functorially related to a map between the collection of vector subspaces of the corresponding spaces.
nodes.label: ex:Vect:3

nodes.name: Down-set
nodes.statement: If $\calX$ is a preorder, a left slice $\Comma{\calX}{a}$ can be interpreted as the set $\SetDef{a' \in \calX}{ a'\leq a }$. This is a sub-preorder of $\calX$, and is called the \emph{down-set} of $a$.
also_stated_at: If $\calX$ is a preorder category, the left or right slice of an object $x$ is the \emph{down-set} or \emph{up-set} of the object.

nodes.name: Group homomorphisms induce order preserving maps between down-sets
nodes.statement: Let $\calX$ be a complete preorder, and $\iota : \calX \to \GroupCat$ a functor that maps $1_{\calX}$ into the trivial group with one object. Let $a,b$ be objects in $\calX$ and $F: \iota(a) \to \iota(b)$ be a group homomorphism. Then $F$ induces an order preserving map $\tau_F$ between the down-sets $\Comma{\calX}{a}$ and $\Comma{\calX}{b}$. Moreover this correspondence is functorial.
assumptions: Let $\calX$ be a complete preorder, and $\iota : \calX \to \GroupCat$ a functor that maps $1_{\calX}$ into the trivial group with one object.
Let $a,b$ be objects in $\calX$ and $F: \iota(a) \to \iota(b)$ be a group homomorphism.
conclusions: $F$ induces an order preserving map $\tau_F$ between the down-sets $\Comma{\calX}{a}$ and $\Comma{\calX}{b}$.
this correspondence is functorial.
nodes.label: corr:6

nodes.name: Singular homology functor
nodes.statement: Recall that singular homology is a functor \[ \text{Homology} : \Topo \to \GroupCat , \] mapping each topological space into its sequence of homology groups.

nodes.name: Simplicial complexes and homology homomorphisms
nodes.statement: Let $\calX$ be a simplicial complex of dimension $n$, comprised of simplices of various dimensions from $0$ to $n$. Each simplex of dimension less than $n$ is included as a face map of a simplex of a higher dimension. Thus $\calX$ is a preorder with a finite number of objects and morphisms contained within $\Topo$. Then for any two faces $a, b$ of $\calX$, the down-sets $\Comma{\calX}{a}$ and $\Comma{\calX}{b}$ are the sub-simplexes of these faces. Any group homomorphism \[ F : \text{Homology}(a) \to \text{Homology}(b) \] induces a unique simplicial map between these sub-complexes whose induced map between the homology groups is precisely $F$.
nodes.label: ex:topo:1

nodes.name: Topological dynamics as set-theoretic dynamics
nodes.statement: Recall the notations from Examples \ref{ex:powset:1}, \ref{ex:powset:2} and \ref{ex:powset:3}. Also recall from Example \ref{ex:dyn_obs} the interpretation of a topological dynamical system as a functor $\Phi: \calT \to \Topo$, where $\calT$ is a semigroup such as $\num_0$, $\integer$ or $\real$. Let us assume without loss of generality that the domain of the dynamics is a subspace of $\calU$. Let $\text{Topo}(\calU)$ denote the subcategory of $\Topo$ generated by all topological subspaces of $\calU$. Then one has the following composable sequence of functors \[\begin{tikzcd} \calT \arrow[rr, "\Phi"] && \text{Topo}(\calU) \arrow[rr, "\Dyn"] && \LSlice{2^{\calU}} \end{tikzcd}\] The composition of these functors is a set-theoretic dynamical system with time semigroup $\calT$. Thus the interpretation of a topological dynamical system as a set-theoretic dynamical system is also functorial.
nodes.statement_short: Composing a topological dynamical system with $\Dyn$ yields a set-theoretic dynamical system, functorially.
nodes.label: ex:powset:4

nodes.name: Orbit of a subset
nodes.statement: Recall that given a dynamical system $\Phi^t : \Omega \to \Omega$ on a space $\Omega$, the orbit of a subset $S\subseteq\Omega$ is the union $\cup_{t\in \calT} \Phi^t(S)$. Alternatively it can be defined to be the smallest subset of $\Omega$ that contains all the images $\Phi^t(S)$.

nodes.name: Orbit functor
nodes.statement: Note that the composite functor $\tilde\Phi : \Dyn \circ \Phi$ from Example \ref{ex:powset:4} leads to a functor $2^{\Omega} \times \calT \to 2^{\Omega}$. Then the orbit of $\Phi$ is the functor shown in the diagram below : \begin{equation} \begin{tikzcd} 2^{\Omega} \times \calT \arrow[d, "\proj_1"'] \arrow[dashed]{drr}[name = n2]{} \arrow{rr}[name = n1]{\tilde\Phi} && 2^{\Omega} \\ 2^{\Omega} \arrow[rr, "\text{Orbit}"] && 2^{\Omega} \arrow[shorten <=1pt, shorten >=1pt, Rightarrow, to path={(n2) to[out=90,in=270] (n1)} ]{ } \end{tikzcd} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The orbit of $\Phi$ is the functor $2^\Omega\to 2^\Omega$ obtained as a right Kan extension of $\tilde\Phi$ along $\proj_1$.

nodes.name: Orbit as a Kan extension diagram
nodes.statement: \begin{tikzcd} 2^{\Omega} \times \calT \arrow[d, "\proj_1"'] \arrow[dashed]{drr}[name = n2]{} \arrow{rr}[name = n1]{\tilde\Phi} && 2^{\Omega} \\ 2^{\Omega} \arrow[rr, "\text{Orbit}"] && 2^{\Omega} \arrow[shorten <=1pt, shorten >=1pt, Rightarrow, to path={(n2) to[out=90,in=270] (n1)} ]{ } \end{tikzcd}
nodes.label: eqn:def:orbit

nodes.name: Categorical orbits of topological dynamical systems
nodes.statement: Every topological dynamical system on a subspace of the universe $\calU$ is a functor $\Phi : \calT \to \Topo(\calU)$. It leads to the following notions : \begin{enumerate} [(i)] \item This functor combines with $\Dyn$ from Theorem \ref{thm:0} to get a dynamical system $\calT \to \LSlice{ 2^{\calU} }$. \item This leads to a functor $\tilde\Phi : 2^{\Omega} \times \calT \to 2^{\Omega}$. \item The existence of the orbit functor follows from the existence of a right Kan extension, as shown in \eqref{eqn:def:orbit}. \item The minimality of the orbit follows from the universal property of a right Kan extension. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: Every topological dynamical system on a subspace of the universe $\calU$ is a functor $\Phi : \calT \to \Topo(\calU)$.
conclusions: This functor combines with $\Dyn$ from Theorem \ref{thm:0} to get a dynamical system $\calT \to \LSlice{ 2^{\calU} }$.
This leads to a functor $\tilde\Phi : 2^{\Omega} \times \calT \to 2^{\Omega}$.
The existence of the orbit functor follows from the existence of a right Kan extension, as shown in \eqref{eqn:def:orbit}.
The minimality of the orbit follows from the universal property of a right Kan extension.
nodes.statement_short: Topological dynamics plus $\Dyn$ give set-level dynamics; the orbit functor exists and is minimal as a right Kan extension.

nodes.name: Assumption A:2 (completeness and initial objects for the general arrangement)
nodes.statement: The category $\calA$ and $\calB$ from \eqref{eqn:abc} are complete, the functor $\beta$ is continuous. Categories $\calA$ and $\calC$ have initial elements $0_{\calA}$ and $0_{\calC}$ respectively, and $\alpha \paran{0_{\calA}} = 0_{\calC}$
nodes.label: A:2

nodes.name: Induced functor
nodes.statement: Assume the arrangement of \eqref{eqn:abc}, and let Assumption \ref{A:2} hold. Fix an object $\alpha a \xrightarrow{F} \beta b$ of the comma category $\Comma{\alpha}{\beta}$. Then there is a functor $\tau_{F} : \Comma{\calA}{a} \to \Comma{\alpha}{\beta}$ such that for any object $a'\xrightarrow{f} a$ in $\Comma{\calA}{a}$, there is an object $b'\xrightarrow{g} b$ in $\Comma{\calB}{b}$, such that the following commutation holds \begin{equation} \begin{tikzcd} a' \arrow[d, "f"'] \\ b \end{tikzcd} \imply \begin{tikzcd} \alpha a' \arrow[d, "\alpha f"'] \arrow[r, "\tau_{F}(f)"] & \beta b' \arrow[d, "\beta g"] \\ \alpha a \arrow[r, "F"'] & \beta b \end{tikzcd} \end{equation} Moreover, $\tau_{F}(f)$ is minimal in the sense for any other object $b'' \xrightarrow{g} b$, if the commutation shown below on the left holds : \[ \begin{tikzcd} \alpha a' \arrow[d, "\alpha f"'] \arrow[r, "\tilde{F}"] & \beta b'' \arrow[d, "\beta g''"] \\ \alpha a \arrow[r, "F"'] & \beta b \end{tikzcd} \imply \begin{tikzcd} & & \beta b' \arrow[ldd, "\beta g'", bend left=50] \arrow[ld, "\beta \phi", dotted] \\ \alpha a' \arrow[d, "\alpha f"'] \arrow[r, "\tilde{F}"'] \arrow[rru, "\tau_{F}(f)", bend left] & \beta b'' \arrow[d, "\beta g''"] & \\ \alpha a \arrow[r, "F"'] & \beta b & \end{tikzcd} \] then there is a unique morphism $b' \xrightarrow{\phi} b''$ such that the commutation on the right holds.
assumptions: Assume the arrangement of \eqref{eqn:abc}, and let Assumption \ref{A:2} hold.
Fix an object $\alpha a \xrightarrow{F} \beta b$ of the comma category $\Comma{\alpha}{\beta}$.
conclusions: there is a functor $\tau_{F} : \Comma{\calA}{a} \to \Comma{\alpha}{\beta}$ such that for any object $a'\xrightarrow{f} a$ in $\Comma{\calA}{a}$, there is an object $b'\xrightarrow{g} b$ in $\Comma{\calB}{b}$, such that the following commutation holds
$\tau_{F}(f)$ is minimal
nodes.statement_short: An object $F:\alpha a\to\beta b$ of the comma category induces a functor $\tau_F$ on the slice over $a$, sending $f$ to a minimal commuting square.
nodes.label: thm:1

nodes.name: Commutation square of tau_F(f)
nodes.statement: \begin{tikzcd} a' \arrow[d, "f"'] \\ b \end{tikzcd} \imply \begin{tikzcd} \alpha a' \arrow[d, "\alpha f"'] \arrow[r, "\tau_{F}(f)"] & \beta b' \arrow[d, "\beta g"] \\ \alpha a \arrow[r, "F"'] & \beta b \end{tikzcd}
nodes.label: eqn:thm:1a

nodes.name: Minimality of tau_F is unsurprising
nodes.statement: \paragraph{Remark} The minimality so described is hardly surprising, since whenever a commutation such as \eqref{eqn:thm:1a} holds, the following commutation also holds \[\begin{tikzcd} & & & \beta b' \arrow[ldd, "\beta g", bend left=50] \arrow[ld, "\beta g", dotted] \\ \alpha a' \arrow[d, "\alpha f"'] \arrow[rr, "\beta g \circ \tau_{F}(f)"'] \arrow[rrru, "\tau_{F}(f)", bend left] & & \beta b \arrow[d, "\beta \Id_{b}"] & \\ \alpha a \arrow[rr, "F"'] & & \beta b & \end{tikzcd}\] This diagram is a special case of the second claim of Theorem \ref{thm:1}, with $\tilde F = \beta g \circ \tau_{F}(f)$ and $\phi=g'$.

nodes.name: Domain of tau_F(f) equals domain of f
nodes.statement: \paragraph{Remark} One of the consequences of Theorem \ref{thm:1} and the commutation in \eqref{eqn:thm:1a} is \[\begin{tikzcd} & & \Comma{\calA}{a} \arrow{dll}[swap]{\Forget_1} \arrow{d}{\tau_F} \\ \calA & & \Comma{\alpha}{\beta} \arrow{ll}{\Forget_1} \end{tikzcd}\] This means that the domain of the arrow $\tau_{F}(f)$ is the same as the domain of the arrow $f$.

nodes.name: Induced functor $\Dyn_F$ between slices
nodes.statement: \paragraph{Remark} Any object $a' \xrightarrow{f} a$ in $\Comma{\calA}{a}$ is sent by $\Forget_1$ into $a'$, whereas it is sent by $\tau_F$ into $\tau_F(f)$, which is then sent by $\Forget_1$ into $a'$. This commutation be extended as follows : \begin{equation} \begin{tikzcd} & & \Comma{\calA}{a} \arrow{rr}{\Dyn_F} \arrow{dll}[swap]{\Forget_1} \arrow{d}{\tau_F} & & \Comma{\calB}{b} \arrow{d}{ \Forget_1 } \\ \calA & & \Comma{\alpha}{\beta} \arrow{ll}{\Forget_1} \arrow{rr}[swap]{\Forget_2} & & \calB \end{tikzcd} \end{equation} The diagram presents a new functor $\Dyn_F$ between the slice categories associated to the terminal points of the comma object $F$.
nodes.statement_short: $\tau_F$ followed by $\Forget_2$ gives a functor $\Dyn_F$ from the slice over $a$ to the slice over $b$.

nodes.name: Definition diagram of Dyn_F
nodes.statement: \begin{tikzcd} & & \Comma{\calA}{a} \arrow{rr}{\Dyn_F} \arrow{dll}[swap]{\Forget_1} \arrow{d}{\tau_F} & & \Comma{\calB}{b} \arrow{d}{ \Forget_1 } \\ \calA & & \Comma{\alpha}{\beta} \arrow{ll}{\Forget_1} \arrow{rr}[swap]{\Forget_2} & & \calB \end{tikzcd}

nodes.statement: The compound objects in $\Comma{ \Forget_2^{ \Comma{\alpha}{\beta} } }{ b }$ lead to a projection functor \[\begin{tikzcd} \Comma{ \Forget_2^{ \Comma{\alpha}{\beta} } }{ b } \arrow[rrr, "\text{Restrict}"'] &&& \Comma{\calB}{b} \end{tikzcd}\]

nodes.statement: Under the same assumptions as Theorem~\ref{thm:1} and the category in \eqref{eqn:eodpc9}. Then there is a functor \[ \bar{\tau}_F : \Comma{\calA}{a} \to \Comma{ \Forget_2^{ \Comma{\alpha}{\beta} } }{ b } \] such that the functors $\tau_{F}$ and $\Dyn_{F}$ are created via composition : \begin{equation} \begin{tikzcd} && \Comma{\calA}{a} \arrow[dll, "\tau_F"', dashed] \arrow[rr, "\Dyn_F", dashed] \arrow[drr, "\bar{\tau}_F"] && \Comma{\calB}{b} \\ \Comma{\alpha}{\beta} && \UR{\alpha}{\beta}{\calB} \arrow[ll, "\Forget_1"] && \Comma{ \Forget_2^{ \Comma{\alpha}{\beta} } }{b} \arrow[ll, "\subseteq"] \arrow[u, "\text{Restrict}"'] \end{tikzcd} \end{equation}
assumptions: Under the same assumptions as Theorem~\ref{thm:1} and the category in \eqref{eqn:eodpc9}.
conclusions: there is a functor \[ \bar{\tau}_F : \Comma{\calA}{a} \to \Comma{ \Forget_2^{ \Comma{\alpha}{\beta} } }{ b } \] such that the functors $\tau_{F}$ and $\Dyn_{F}$ are created via composition
nodes.statement_short: A single functor $\bar\tau_F$ into the comma category over $b$ yields both $\tau_F$ and $\Dyn_F$ by composition.
nodes.label: thm:2

nodes.name: Composition diagram for tau_F and Dyn_F
nodes.statement: \begin{tikzcd} && \Comma{\calA}{a} \arrow[dll, "\tau_F"', dashed] \arrow[rr, "\Dyn_F", dashed] \arrow[drr, "\bar{\tau}_F"] && \Comma{\calB}{b} \\ \Comma{\alpha}{\beta} && \UR{\alpha}{\beta}{\calB} \arrow[ll, "\Forget_1"] && \Comma{ \Forget_2^{ \Comma{\alpha}{\beta} } }{b} \arrow[ll, "\subseteq"] \arrow[u, "\text{Restrict}"'] \end{tikzcd}
nodes.label: eqn:thm:2

nodes.name: Induced functor for arrow categories is post-composition
nodes.statement: \paragraph{Remark} When $\calA = \calB = \calC$ in \eqref{eqn:abc}, and $\alpha = \beta = \Id_{\calA}$, then $\Comma{\alpha}{\beta}$ is just the arrow category $\ArrowCat{\calA}$. Any object $a \xrightarrow{F} b$ in this category induces a functor between the slice categories : \[\begin{tikzcd} x \arrow[r, "f", Holud] \arrow[d, "\phi"', Itranga] & a \\ x' \arrow[ru, "f'"', Akashi] & \end{tikzcd} \quad \begin{tikzcd} {} \arrow[rrr, mapsto] &&& {} \end{tikzcd} \quad \begin{tikzcd} x \arrow[rrd, Holud, dashed, bend left = 20] \arrow[rd, "f"] \arrow[dd, "\phi"', Itranga] \\ & a \arrow{r}{F} & b \\ x' \arrow[rru, Akashi, dashed, bend right = 20] \arrow[ru, "f'"'] & \end{tikzcd}\] The yellow and blue arrows represent different objects in the respective slice categories, and the red arrows represent morphisms between these objects. The diagram on the right is obtained from the left by simply composing with $F$. This functorial relation coincides with $\tau_F$.
nodes.statement_short: When all functors are identities, $\tau_F$ is simply post-composition with $F$ between slices.

nodes.name: Factorization systems approach to induced functors
nodes.statement: \paragraph{Remark} While $\tau_F$ has a simple interpretation when all the functors in \eqref{eqn:abc} are identities, determining an induced functor in the more general setting is not trivial. One notable approach relies on the existence of special factorization systems \citep[e.g.][]{adamek1990abstract, FreydKelly1972cont1}. This approach has been extended to an axiomatic study of topology \cite{Schlomiuk1970topo, ClementinoGiuliTholen1996, DikranjanGiuli1987closure, DikranjanTholen2013clos}.

nodes.name: Induced morphisms are surjective
nodes.statement: Assumptions \ref{A:1} and \ref{A:3} hold. Then the induced morphisms $\tau_F(f)$ from Theorem \ref{thm:1} are surjective.
assumptions: Assumptions \ref{A:1} and \ref{A:3} hold.
conclusions: the induced morphisms $\tau_F(f)$ from Theorem \ref{thm:1} are surjective.
nodes.label: thm:3

nodes.name: Equalizers are monomorphisms
nodes.statement: In any category, an equalizer is injective.
assumptions: In any category
conclusions: an equalizer is injective.
nodes.label: lem:Eq_inj

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem thm:3
nodes.statement: \paragraph{Proof of Theorem \ref{thm:3}} To prove surjectivity we need to show that for any pair of morphisms $\alpha, \beta : \iota B \to C$, if $\alpha \circ \tau_F{f} = \beta \circ \tau_F{f}$ then $\alpha = \beta$. Since $\calY$ is complete it has equalizers. Consider the following diagram in which the equalizer of $\alpha, \beta$ has been shown. \[\begin{tikzcd} & D \arrow{d}{\text{Eq}(\alpha, \beta)"} \arrow[rrd, bend left] & & \\ \iota A \arrow[r, "\tau_F(a)"'] \arrow[ru, "\exists! \phi", dotted] & \iota B \arrow[r, "\alpha"'] \arrow[rd, "\beta"', bend right] & C & C \arrow[l, "\cong"] \arrow[ld, "\cong", bend left] \\ & & C & \end{tikzcd}\] Since the equalizer is by definition, the universal morphism $\gamma$ such that $\beta \gamma = \alpha \gamma$, the morphism $\tau_F(f)$ must factor through the equalizer via the morphism $\phi$ as shown. Now by Lemma \ref{lem:Eq_inj}, the morphism $\text{Eq}(\alpha, \beta)$ is injective. By Assumption \ref{A:3}, $\text{Eq}(\alpha, \beta)$ factorizes as shown below. \[\begin{tikzcd} & & D \arrow{d}{\text{Eq}(\alpha, \beta)"} \arrow[rr, "f"] & & \iota E \arrow[lld, "\iota \psi"] \\ \iota A \arrow[rr, "\tau_F(a)"'] \arrow[rru, "\phi"] & & \iota B & & \end{tikzcd}\] This commutation diagram can be joined with the definition of $\tau_F(f)$ to get \[\begin{tikzcd} & & D \arrow{d}{\text{Eq}(\alpha, \beta)"} \arrow[rr, "f"] & & \iota E \arrow[lld, "\iota \psi"] \arrow[lldd, "\iota (b\circ \psi)", dotted, bend left] \\ \iota A \arrow[rr, "\tau_F(a)"'] \arrow[rru, "\phi"] \arrow[d, "\iota a"'] \arrow[rrrru, dashed, bend left=50] & & \iota B \arrow[d, "\iota b"] & & \\ \iota \Omega \arrow[rr, "F"'] & & \iota \Omega' & & \end{tikzcd}\] By the universality of $\tau_F(f)$, the morphism $\psi$ must be an isomorphism. This would mean that $\text{Eq}(\alpha, \beta)$ is an isomorphism too. This in turn implies that $\alpha=\beta$, which was our goal. This completes the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:3}. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Factor $\tau_F(f)$ through the equalizer of $\alpha,\beta$; by Assumption A:3 and universality the equalizer is an iso, so $\alpha=\beta$.

nodes.name: Compositionality of induced functors
nodes.statement: Suppose Assumptions \ref{A:1} \ref{A:4} and \ref{A:5} hold. Then there is a functor \[ \iota(\calX) \xrightarrow{\tau} \LSlice{ \calX } , \] which maps an arrow $\iota \Omega \xrightarrow{F} \iota \Omega'$ into $\Comma{\calX}{\Omega} \xrightarrow{\tau_F} \Comma{\calX}{\Omega'}$.
assumptions: Suppose Assumptions \ref{A:1} \ref{A:4} and \ref{A:5} hold.
conclusions: there is a functor \[ \iota(\calX) \xrightarrow{\tau} \LSlice{ \calX } , \] which maps an arrow $\iota \Omega \xrightarrow{F} \iota \Omega'$ into $\Comma{\calX}{\Omega} \xrightarrow{\tau_F} \Comma{\calX}{\Omega'}$.
nodes.statement_short: The assignment $F\mapsto\tau_F$ is functorial from $\iota(\calX)$ to the category of left slices.
nodes.label: thm:4

nodes.name: Compositionality diagram
nodes.statement: \paragraph{Remark} Theorem \ref{thm:4} essentially says that the correspondence of $\Dyn_F$ with $F$ preserves composition. This leads to the following diagram : \[ \begin{tikzcd} \iota \Omega \arrow[dashed, bend right = 40]{dd}[swap]{F'\circ F} \arrow{d}{F} \\ \iota \Omega' \arrow{d}{F'} \\ \iota \Omega'' \end{tikzcd} \imply \begin{tikzcd} \Comma{\calX}{\Omega} \arrow[d, "\tau_F"] \arrow[rr, "\Dyn_F"] \arrow[dd, "\tau_{F'\circ F}"', bend right=49] \arrow[rrrr, "\Dyn_{F'\circ F}", bend left=30] & & \Comma{\calX}{\Omega'} \arrow[d, "\tau_F"] \arrow[ld, "\Forget_1"'] \arrow[rr, "\Dyn_{F'}"] & & \Comma{\calX}{\Omega''} \arrow[ld, "\Forget_21"'] \arrow[dd, "\Forget_1"] \\ \Comma{\iota}{\iota} \arrow[r, "\Forget_2"] & \calX & \Comma{\iota}{\iota} \arrow[r, "\Forget_2"] & \calX & \\ \Comma{\iota}{\iota} \arrow[rrrr, "\Forget_2"] & & & & \calX \end{tikzcd}\] The upper commuting loop is the statement of Theorem \ref{thm:4}. The outer commutating loop, along with the two smaller loops are a consequence of \eqref{eqn:def:Dyn}.

nodes.name: Right cancellation of epimorphisms
nodes.statement: In any category $\calC$, if $f,g$ are two composable morphisms such that $f, g\circ f$ are surjective, then $g$ is also surjective.
assumptions: In any category $\calC$, if $f,g$ are two composable morphisms such that $f, g\circ f$ are surjective
conclusions: $g$ is also surjective.
nodes.label: lem:surj_right_cancel

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma lem:surj_right_cancel
nodes.statement: We need to shown that for any morphisms $\alpha, \beta$ such that $\alpha g = \beta g$, $\alpha$ must equal $\beta$. Now note that \[ \alpha \paran{g f} = \paran{\alpha g} f = \paran{\beta g} f = \beta \paran{gf} . \] Since $gf$ is surjective, we must have $\alpha=\beta$, proving the claim.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite $\alpha(gf)=\beta(gf)$ by associativity and cancel the epimorphism $gf$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem thm:4
nodes.statement: \paragraph{Proof of Theorem \ref{thm:4}} We start with the following setup : \[\begin{tikzcd} \iota A \arrow[d, "\iota a"'] \\ \iota \Omega \arrow[rr, "F"'] & & \iota \Omega' \arrow[rr, "F'"'] & & \iota \Omega'' & \end{tikzcd}\] This contains an object $A\in \Comma{\calX}{\Omega}$, and two composable arrows $F, F' \in \Comma{\iota}{\iota}$. We can apply the functors $\tau_F$ and $\tau_{F'}$ in succession to get \[\begin{tikzcd} \iota A \arrow[d, "\iota a"'] \arrow[rr, "\tau_{F} (a)"] & & \iota B \arrow[d, "\iota b"] \arrow[rr, "\tau_{F'} (b)"] & & \iota C \arrow[d, "\iota c"'] & \\ \iota \Omega \arrow[rr, "F"'] & & \iota \Omega' \arrow[rr, "F'"'] & & \iota \Omega'' & \end{tikzcd}\] To prove Theorem \ref{thm:4}, it has to be shown that the composition along the arrows in the upper row equals $\tau_{F'\circ F}$. The object $\tau_{F'\circ F}(a)$ itself can be drawn as shown below : \[\begin{tikzcd} & & & & & \iota D \arrow[ldd, "\iota d", bend left] \arrow[ld, "! \iota \phi"'] \\ \iota A \arrow[d, "\iota a"'] \arrow[rr, "\tau_{F} (a)"] \arrow[rrrrru, "\tau_{F'\circ F} (a)", bend left] & & \iota B \arrow[d, "\iota b"] \arrow[rr, "\tau_{F'} (b)"] & & \iota C \arrow[d, "\iota c"'] & \\ \iota \Omega \arrow[rr, "F"'] & & \iota \Omega' \arrow[rr, "F'"'] & & \iota \Omega'' & \end{tikzcd}\] The connecting morphism $\phi : D \to C$ exists by the minimality of $\tau_{F'\circ F}(a)$. The upper commuting loop can be expressed as \[ \tau_{F'} (b) \circ \tau_{F} (a) = \iota \phi \circ \tau_{F'\circ F} (a) . \] By Theorem \ref{thm:3}, all the three morphisms $\tau_{F} (a)$, $\tau_{F'} (b)$ and $\tau_{F'\circ F} (a)$ are surjective. Thus by Lemma \ref{lem:surj_right_cancel}, $\iota \phi$ must be surjective too. By Assumption \ref{A:4} $\iota \phi$ is also injective. Thus by Assumption \ref{A:5}, $\iota \phi$ is an isomorphism. This implies that $\tau_{F'} (b) \circ \tau_{F} (a)$ and $\tau_{F'\circ F} (a)$ are equal up to isomorphism. This completes the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:4}. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Compare $\tau_{F'}(b)\circ\tau_F(a)$ with $\tau_{F'\circ F}(a)$ via the minimality map $\iota\phi$. Surjectivity (Thm thm:3), right cancellation and Assumptions A:4, A:5 make $\iota\phi$ an isomorphism.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem thm:0
nodes.statement: \paragraph{Proof of Theorem \ref{thm:0}} Note that Assumption \ref{A:1} in Theorem \ref{thm:0} is a special case of Assumption \ref{A:2}. As a result we can build the induced functors $\bar{\tau}_F$ and $\tau_F$ from Theorems \ref{thm:1} and \ref{thm:2} respectively. Since $\iota$ is assumed to be injective on objects, the objects of $\iota(\calX)$ are in bijection with the object of $\calX$. Thus each object in $\iota(\calX)$ corresponds to a unique image $\iota \Omega$, for some $\Omega \in ob(\calX)$. The functoriality now follows from Theorem \ref{thm:4}. This completes the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:0}. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Assumption A:1 specializes A:2, so Theorems thm:1, thm:2 give $\tau_F$; injectivity on objects and Theorem thm:4 give functoriality.

nodes.statement: A particular instance of \eqref{eqn:gpd30} is shown in the center below, \begin{equation} \input{ MapC_Def.tex} \end{equation} The leftmost figure in \eqref{eqn:def:MapC} is an object $F$ in $\Comma{\alpha}{\beta}$. The middle diagram presents a simple commutation in which this object is re-interpreted as a functor. Finally, the leftmost figure presents an application of Proposition \ref{lem:gpd30} to this commutation. The dashed arrow in the above diagram indicate that it is are defined via composition. nodes.name: Right inverse as right adjoint
nodes.statement: Suppose $F:\calP \to \calQ$ and $G:\calQ \to \calP$ are two functors such that $FG = \Id_{\calQ}$ and $\Id_{\calP} \Rightarrow GF$. Then $F,G$ are left and right adjoints of each other.
assumptions: $F:\calP \to \calQ$ and $G:\calQ \to \calP$ are two functors such that $FG = \Id_{\calQ}$ and $\Id_{\calP} \Rightarrow GF$.
conclusions: $F,G$ are left and right adjoints of each other.
nodes.label: lem:RIRA

nodes.name: Left adjoint of the second forgetful functor
nodes.statement: Consider an arrangement of categories and functors $\calP \xrightarrow{P} \calR \xleftarrow{Q} \calQ$. If $\calP$ and $\calQ$ have initial elements $0_{\calP}$ and $1_{\calQ}$ respectively, and $P \paran{0_{\calP}} = 0_{\calR}$, then the functor $\Forget_2 : \Comma{P}{Q}$ has a left adjoint given by \[ \paran{ \Forget_2 }^{(L)} : \calQ \to \Comma{P}{Q}, \quad q \mapsto \; \begin{tikzcd} P 0_{\calP} = 0_{\calR} \arrow[d, "!_{Qq}"] \\ Qq \end{tikzcd} \] In fact, $\paran{ \Forget_1 }^{(L)}$ is a right inverse of $\Forget_1$, i.e., $\Forget_2 \circ \paran{ \Forget_2 }^{(L)} = \Id_{\calQ}$.
assumptions: Consider an arrangement of categories and functors $\calP \xrightarrow{P} \calR \xleftarrow{Q} \calQ$.
$\calP$ and $\calQ$ have initial elements $0_{\calP}$ and $1_{\calQ}$ respectively, and $P \paran{0_{\calP}} = 0_{\calR}$
conclusions: the functor $\Forget_2 : \Comma{P}{Q}$ has a left adjoint
$\paran{ \Forget_1 }^{(L)}$ is a right inverse of $\Forget_1$, i.e., $\Forget_2 \circ \paran{ \Forget_2 }^{(L)} = \Id_{\calQ}$.
nodes.statement_short: If $P$ preserves initial objects, $\Forget_2$ on $\Comma{P}{Q}$ has a left adjoint sending $q$ to the initial arrow into $Qq$.
nodes.label: lem:frgt_adjnt

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma lem:frgt_adjnt
nodes.statement: Since $\paran{ \Forget_1 }^{(R)}$ is a right inverse of $\Forget_1$ by Lemma \ref{lem:RIRA}, it only remains to be shown that there is a natural transformation $\paran{ \Forget_2 }^{(L)} \circ \Forget_2 \Rightarrow \Id_{\Comma{P}{Q}}$, called the \emph{counit}. The diagram on the left below traces the action of this composite functor on an object $F$ (blue) of $\Comma{P}{Q}$ into an object (green) of $\Comma{P}{Q}$ : \[\begin{tikzcd} Pp \arrow[d, "F"', Akashi] \\ Qq \end{tikzcd} \;\begin{tikzcd} {} \arrow[rr, mapsto, "\Forget_2"] && {} \end{tikzcd} \; q \;\begin{tikzcd} {} \arrow[rr, mapsto, "\paran{ \Forget_2 }^{(L)}"] && {} \end{tikzcd} \; \begin{tikzcd} P 0_{\calP} = 0_{\calR} \arrow[d, "!_{Qq}", Shobuj] \\ Qq \end{tikzcd} ; \quad \begin{tikzcd} P0_{\calP} \arrow[d, "P(!_p)"', Holud] \arrow[r, "!_{Qq}", Shobuj] & Qq \arrow[d, "Q \Id_q", Holud]\\ Pp \arrow[r, "F", Akashi] & Qq \end{tikzcd}\] The diagram on the left demonstrates a commutation arising out of the initial element preserving property. The descending yellow morphisms together constitute the connecting morphism of the counit transformation we seek. This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma lem:RIRA it suffices to build the counit; its components come from the initial-object-preserving commutation.

nodes.name: Left adjoint of the forgetful functor from UR
nodes.statement: In the arrangement of \eqref{eqn:abc}, the forgetful functor \[ \Forget_{1} : \UR{\alpha}{\beta}{\calB} := \Comma{ \Forget_2^{ \Comma{\alpha}{\beta} } }{ \Id_{\calB} } \to \Comma{\alpha}{\beta} , \] has a left adjoint \[ \Forget_{1}^{(L)} : \Comma{\alpha}{\beta} \to \UR{\alpha}{\beta}{\calB} , \quad \begin{tikzcd} \alpha a \arrow[d, "F"'] \\ \beta b \end{tikzcd} \; \begin{tikzcd} {} \arrow[rr, mapsto] && {} \end{tikzcd} \; \begin{tikzcd} \alpha a \arrow[r, "F"'] & \beta b \arrow[d, "\beta \Id_b"]\\ & \beta b \end{tikzcd} . \]
nodes.statement_short: The forgetful functor from $\UR{\alpha}{\beta}{\calB}$ to $\Comma{\alpha}{\beta}$ has a left adjoint appending $\beta\Id_b$.
nodes.label: lem:jd9lk3

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma lem:jd9lk3
nodes.statement: The functor $\Forget_{1}^{(L)}$ is clearly a right inverse of $\Forget_{1}$. Thus again by Lemma \ref{lem:RIRA} , it is enough to show the existence of a natural transformation as shown on the left below : \[ \eta : \Forget_1^{(L)} \circ \Forget_1 \Rightarrow \Id , \quad \begin{tikzcd} \alpha a \arrow[d, "F"', Akashi] \\ \beta b \end{tikzcd}, \, \begin{tikzcd} b \arrow[d, "\phi"', Akashi] \\ b' \end{tikzcd} , \; \begin{tikzcd} {} \arrow[rr, "\eta", mapsto] && {} \end{tikzcd} \; \begin{tikzcd} & \alpha a \arrow[r, "F", Holud] \arrow[ld, "="] & \beta b \arrow[ld, "="'] \arrow[d, "\beta \Id_b", Holud] & \\ \alpha a \arrow[r, "F"', Akashi] & \beta b \arrow[d, "\phi"', Akashi] & \beta b \arrow[ld, "\phi"] & \\ & \beta b' & & \end{tikzcd}\] The connecting morphisms of this natural transformation is shown above on the right.
nodes.statement_short: The candidate is a right inverse; by Lemma lem:RIRA it suffices to exhibit the natural transformation $\eta$.

nodes.name: Functors into UR over a fixed b factor through the slice over b
nodes.statement: Recall the inclusion functor from \eqref{eqn:0lkd0e}. It leads to a pull-back square : \[\begin{tikzcd} \Comma{\Forget_2^{ \Comma{\alpha}{\beta}}}{b} \arrow[r, "\subset"] \arrow[d, ""] & \UR{\alpha}{\beta}{\calB} \arrow[d, "\Forget_2"] \\ \star \arrow[r, "b"'] & \calB \end{tikzcd}\] Now consider any functor $\calT: \calP \to \UR{\alpha}{\beta}{\calB}$ such that $\Forget_2 \circ \calT \equiv b$, for some object $b$ of $\calB$. Then the commutation on the left below is satisfied : \begin{equation} \begin{tikzcd} \calP \arrow[r, "\calT"] \arrow[d, ""] & \UR{\alpha}{\beta}{\calB} \arrow[d, "\Forget_2"] \\ \star \arrow[r, "b"'] & \calB \end{tikzcd} \imply \begin{tikzcd} \calP \arrow[drr, "\calT", bend left=20] \arrow[ddr, "", bend right=20] \arrow[Akashi, dr, "\calT'"] \arrow[Akashi, dd, "\calT''"', dashed] \\ & \Comma{\Forget_2^{ \Comma{\alpha}{\beta}}}{b} \arrow[dl, Holud, "\text{Restrict}"] \arrow[r, "\subset"] \arrow[d, ""] & \UR{\alpha}{\beta}{\calB} \arrow[d, "\Forget_2"] \\ \Comma{\calB}{b} & \star \arrow[r, "b"'] & \calB \end{tikzcd} \end{equation} This commutation must factor through the pullback square as shown by the blue arrow in the diagram in the middle. Thus given any functor $\calT$ as above, \eqref{eqn:T_T2_T3} says that $\calT$ factors through a map $\calT'$ mapping into $\Comma{\Forget_2^{ \Comma{\alpha}{\beta}}}{b}$, a subcategory of $\UR{\alpha}{\beta}{\calB}$. Since the category $\Comma{\Forget_2^{ \Comma{\alpha}{\beta}}}{b}$ can be further restricted to the slice $\Comma{\calB}{b}$, $\calT'$ extends to a functor mapping into $\Comma{\calB}{b}$.
nodes.statement_short: A functor into UR whose second projection is constant at $b$ factors through the pullback $\Comma{\Forget_2}{b}$, hence maps into the slice over $b$.

nodes.statement: \begin{tikzcd} \calP \arrow[r, "\calT"] \arrow[d, ""] & \UR{\alpha}{\beta}{\calB} \arrow[d, "\Forget_2"] \\ \star \arrow[r, "b"'] & \calB \end{tikzcd} \imply \begin{tikzcd} \calP \arrow[drr, "\calT", bend left=20] \arrow[ddr, "", bend right=20] \arrow[Akashi, dr, "\calT'"] \arrow[Akashi, dd, "\calT''"', dashed] \\ & \Comma{\Forget_2^{ \Comma{\alpha}{\beta}}}{b} \arrow[dl, Holud, "\text{Restrict}"] \arrow[r, "\subset"] \arrow[d, ""] & \UR{\alpha}{\beta}{\calB} \arrow[d, "\Forget_2"] \\ \Comma{\calB}{b} & \star \arrow[r, "b"'] & \calB \end{tikzcd}

nodes.statement: \citep[][Thm 4.5.3]{Riehl_context_2017} If a functor $F:\calP\to \calQ$ has a left adjoint, then for any diagram $\Psi : J\to \calP$, if $\lim \psi$ exists, then $\lim (F\circ \Psi) = F \paran{ \lim \Psi }$.

$\lim \psi$ exists
conclusions: $\lim (F\circ \Psi) = F \paran{ \lim \Psi }$

nodes.name: Pre construction at an object $\Pre{F}{G}(y)$
nodes.statement: Consider an arrangement $\calY \xleftarrow{F} \calX \xrightarrow{G} \calZ$. Given an object $y$ of $\calY$, one can create the composite functor : \begin{equation} \begin{tikzcd} \Comma{F}{y} \arrow[dashed]{rr}{ \green{ \Pre{F}{G}(y) } } \arrow{d}[swap]{ \Forget_{ \Comma{F}{y} } } && Z \\ X \times \{\star\} \arrow{rr}{\cong} && X \arrow{u}[swap]{ G } \end{tikzcd} \end{equation}

nodes.name: Composite functor Pre_{F,G}(y)
nodes.statement: \begin{tikzcd} \Comma{F}{y} \arrow[dashed]{rr}{ \green{ \Pre{F}{G}(y) } } \arrow{d}[swap]{ \Forget_{ \Comma{F}{y} } } && Z \\ X \times \{\star\} \arrow{rr}{\cong} && X \arrow{u}[swap]{ G } \end{tikzcd}

nodes.name: Pre functor $\Pre{F}{G}$
nodes.statement: This gives us a functor \begin{equation} \Pre{F}{G} : Y \to \Comma{ \CatCat }{Z}, \; y\mapsto \paran{ \Comma{F}{y}, \Pre{F}{G}(y) } ;\; \begin{tikzcd} y \arrow{d}{\psi} \\ y' \end{tikzcd} \,\mapsto\, \begin{tikzcd} \Comma{F}{y} \arrow[bend left=20]{drr}{ \Pre{F}{G}(y) } \arrow[bend right=10]{dr}{ \Forget_{ \Comma{F}{y} } } \arrow{dd}{\psi\circ}\\ & X \arrow{r}{G} & Z\\ \Comma{F}{y'} \arrow[bend left=10]{ur}[swap]{ \Forget_{ \Comma{F}{y'} } } \arrow[bend right=20]{urr}[swap]{ \Pre{F}{G}(y') } \end{tikzcd} \end{equation}

nodes.statement: \Pre{F}{G} : Y \to \Comma{ \CatCat }{Z}, \; y\mapsto \paran{ \Comma{F}{y}, \Pre{F}{G}(y) } ;\; \begin{tikzcd} y \arrow{d}{\psi} \\ y' \end{tikzcd} \,\mapsto\, \begin{tikzcd} \Comma{F}{y} \arrow[bend left=20]{drr}{ \Pre{F}{G}(y) } \arrow[bend right=10]{dr}{ \Forget_{ \Comma{F}{y} } } \arrow{dd}{\psi\circ}\\ & X \arrow{r}{G} & Z\\ \Comma{F}{y'} \arrow[bend left=10]{ur}[swap]{ \Forget_{ \Comma{F}{y'} } } \arrow[bend right=20]{urr}[swap]{ \Pre{F}{G}(y') } \end{tikzcd}

nodes.name: Limit functor on diagrams
nodes.statement: Given a complete category $\calZ$, there is a functor $\lim : \Comma{\CatCat}{\calZ} \to \calZ$ which maps each diagram $F:J\to \calZ$ into $\lim F$.
assumptions: Given a complete category $\calZ$
conclusions: there is a functor $\lim : \Comma{\CatCat}{\calZ} \to \calZ$ which maps each diagram $F:J\to \calZ$ into $\lim F$.
nodes.label: lem:id30l

nodes.name: LimPre construction
nodes.statement: For a complete category $\calZ$, the $\lim$ functor can be used to extend the functor from \eqref{eqn:def:Pre}, as shown below : \begin{equation} \begin{tikzcd} \calY \arrow[drr, Shobuj, "\LimPre_{F,G}"'] \arrow[rr, "b"] && \Comma{ \CatCat }{Z} \arrow[d, "\lim"] \\ && \calZ \end{tikzcd} \end{equation} This construction $\LimPre_{F,G}$ is one of the main innovations in this paper. The use of colimits instead of limits would have yielded the right Kan extension of $F$ along $G$. for any object $y$ of $\calY$, $\LimPre_{F,G}(y)$ is the limit point of the functor $G$ restricted to the left slice $\Comma{F}{y}$.
nodes.statement_short: $\LimPre_{F,G}(y)$ is the limit of $G$ restricted to the slice $\Comma{F}{y}$, i.e. $\lim\circ\Pre{F}{G}$.

nodes.name: LimPre as lim composed with Pre
nodes.statement: \begin{tikzcd} \calY \arrow[drr, Shobuj, "\LimPre_{F,G}"'] \arrow[rr, "b"] && \Comma{ \CatCat }{Z} \arrow[d, "\lim"] \\ && \calZ \end{tikzcd}
nodes.label: eqn:LimPre

nodes.name: Limit preserving functor
nodes.statement: Given two complete categories $\calZ, \calZ'$ a functor $\Psi : \calZ \to \calZ'$ is called \emph{limit preserving} if the following commutation holds : \begin{equation} \begin{tikzcd} \Comma{\CatCat}{\calZ} \arrow[d, "\lim"'] \arrow[r, "F\circ"] & \Comma{\CatCat}{\calZ'} \arrow[d, "\lim"] \\ \calQ \arrow[r, "F"] & \calZ' \end{tikzcd} \end{equation}

nodes.name: Limit preservation commutation
nodes.statement: \begin{tikzcd} \Comma{\CatCat}{\calZ} \arrow[d, "\lim"'] \arrow[r, "F\circ"] & \Comma{\CatCat}{\calZ'} \arrow[d, "\lim"] \\ \calQ \arrow[r, "F"] & \calZ' \end{tikzcd}
nodes.label: eqn:svo02l

nodes.name: LimPre commutes with limit preserving functors
nodes.statement: Given an arrangement of functors \[\begin{tikzcd} \calR & \calP \arrow[r, "Q"] \arrow[l, "R"'] & \calQ \arrow[r, "F"] & \calQ' \end{tikzcd}\] in which $F$ is limit preserving, the following commutation holds between the $\LimPre$ functors : \[\begin{tikzcd} \calP \arrow[rrr, bend left=30, "F\circ Q"] \arrow[rr, "Q"'] \arrow[d, "R"'] && \calQ \arrow[r, "F"'] & \calQ' \\ \calR \arrow[rrr, bend right=30, "\LimPre_{R,F\circ Q}"'] \arrow[rr, "\LimPre_{R,Q}"] && \calQ \arrow[r, "F"] & \calQ' \end{tikzcd}\]
nodes.statement_short: Post-composing with a limit-preserving $F$ commutes with the $\LimPre$ construction.
nodes.label: lem:LimPre:extend

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma lem:LimPre:extend
nodes.statement: Note that for every $y\in ob(\calY)$, \[\begin{split} \LimPre_{R,F\circ Q} (y) &= \lim \Pre{R}{F\circ Q}(y) = \lim \Pre{R}{F\circ \Pre{R}Q}(y) \\ & = F\circ \lim \Pre{R}{\Pre{R}Q}(y) = F\circ \LimPre_{R,Q} (y) , \end{split}\] where the second last inequality holds from the limit preservation property.
nodes.statement_short: Unfold $\LimPre$ as $\lim\circ\Pre{}{}$ and pull $F$ out using limit preservation.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorems thm:1 and thm:2
nodes.statement: The proofs of the two theorems shall be derived simultaneously. We begin the proof by drawing a portion of \eqref{eqn:ArrowComma3}. \[\begin{tikzcd} [] \ArrowCat{ \Comma{\alpha}{\beta} } \arrow[dd, "DL"'] \arrow[rr, "UR", Shobuj] \arrow[bend left = 30, Holud, "\Forget_1", rrrr] && \UR{\alpha}{\beta}{\calB} \arrow[rr, "\Forget_1"] && \Comma{\alpha}{\beta} \\ && && && \\ \DL{\alpha}{\beta}{\calA} \end{tikzcd}\] Since the categories $\Comma{\alpha}{\beta}$ and $\UR{\alpha}{\beta}{\calB}$ are complete by Lemmas \ref{lem:comma_cocmplt} and \ref{lem:UR_cmplt} respectively, we can create the $\LimPre$ constructions of these functors, as shown below : \[\begin{tikzcd} [] \ArrowCat{ \Comma{\alpha}{\beta} } \arrow[dd, "DL"'] \arrow[rr, "UR", Shobuj] \arrow[bend left = 30, Holud, "\Forget_1", rrrr] && \UR{\alpha}{\beta}{\calB} \arrow[rr, "\Forget_1"] && \Comma{\alpha}{\beta} \\ && && && \\ \DL{\alpha}{\beta}{\calA} \arrow[rrrr, bend right=20, Holud, dotted, "\gamma_F"'] \arrow[rr, "\bar{\gamma}_F"', Shobuj, dotted] && \UR{\alpha}{\beta}{\calB} \arrow[rr, "\Forget_1"] && \Comma{\alpha}{\beta} \end{tikzcd}\] Each colored dotted arrow is the $\LimPre$ construction corresponding to the functor of the same color on the top row. The commutation between the $\LimPre$ constructions in the second row holds by Lemma \ref{lem:frgt_adjnt}, Lemma \ref{lem:jd9lk3} and Lemma \ref{lem:LimPre:extend}. nodes.name: Reduce surjectivity to cancellation
nodes.statement: \paragraph{Proof of Theorem \ref{thm:3}} To prove surjectivity we need to show that for any pair of morphisms $\alpha, \beta : \iota B \to C$, if $\alpha \circ \tau_F{f} = \beta \circ \tau_F{f}$ then $\alpha = \beta$.
nodes.statement_short: State what must be shown: right cancellation of $\tau_F(f)$.

nodes.name: Factor through the equalizer
nodes.statement: Since $\calY$ is complete it has equalizers. Consider the following diagram in which the equalizer of $\alpha, \beta$ has been shown. \[\begin{tikzcd} & D \arrow{d}{\text{Eq}(\alpha, \beta)"} \arrow[rrd, bend left] & & \\ \iota A \arrow[r, "\tau_F(a)"'] \arrow[ru, "\exists! \phi", dotted] & \iota B \arrow[r, "\alpha"'] \arrow[rd, "\beta"', bend right] & C & C \arrow[l, "\cong"] \arrow[ld, "\cong", bend left] \\ & & C & \end{tikzcd}\] Since the equalizer is by definition, the universal morphism $\gamma$ such that $\beta \gamma = \alpha \gamma$, the morphism $\tau_F(f)$ must factor through the equalizer via the morphism $\phi$ as shown.
nodes.statement_short: Use completeness to form the equalizer and factor $\tau_F(f)$ through it.

nodes.name: Equalizer is mono and factors through iota
nodes.statement: Now by Lemma \ref{lem:Eq_inj}, the morphism $\text{Eq}(\alpha, \beta)$ is injective. By Assumption \ref{A:3}, $\text{Eq}(\alpha, \beta)$ factorizes as shown below. \[\begin{tikzcd} & & D \arrow{d}{\text{Eq}(\alpha, \beta)"} \arrow[rr, "f"] & & \iota E \arrow[lld, "\iota \psi"] \\ \iota A \arrow[rr, "\tau_F(a)"'] \arrow[rru, "\phi"] & & \iota B & & \end{tikzcd}\]
nodes.statement_short: Equalizer is injective (Lemma lem:Eq_inj) and factors via Assumption A:3.

nodes.name: Universality forces psi iso
nodes.statement: This commutation diagram can be joined with the definition of $\tau_F(f)$ to get \[\begin{tikzcd} & & D \arrow{d}{\text{Eq}(\alpha, \beta)"} \arrow[rr, "f"] & & \iota E \arrow[lld, "\iota \psi"] \arrow[lldd, "\iota (b\circ \psi)", dotted, bend left] \\ \iota A \arrow[rr, "\tau_F(a)"'] \arrow[rru, "\phi"] \arrow[d, "\iota a"'] \arrow[rrrru, dashed, bend left=50] & & \iota B \arrow[d, "\iota b"] & & \\ \iota \Omega \arrow[rr, "F"'] & & \iota \Omega' & & \end{tikzcd}\] By the universality of $\tau_F(f)$, the morphism $\psi$ must be an isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Combine with the defining square of $\tau_F(f)$; universality makes $\psi$ an isomorphism.

nodes.name: Conclude alpha = beta
nodes.statement: This would mean that $\text{Eq}(\alpha, \beta)$ is an isomorphism too. This in turn implies that $\alpha=\beta$, which was our goal. This completes the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:3}. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Equalizer is an isomorphism, so $\alpha=\beta$.

nodes.name: Goal: right cancellation
nodes.statement: We need to shown that for any morphisms $\alpha, \beta$ such that $\alpha g = \beta g$, $\alpha$ must equal $\beta$.
nodes.statement_short: State the cancellation property to prove.

nodes.name: Associativity
nodes.statement: Now note that \[ \alpha \paran{g f} = \paran{\alpha g} f = \paran{\beta g} f = \beta \paran{gf} . \]
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite using associativity.

nodes.name: Cancel gf
nodes.statement: Since $gf$ is surjective, we must have $\alpha=\beta$, proving the claim.
nodes.statement_short: Cancel the epimorphism $gf$.

nodes.name: Setup
nodes.statement: \paragraph{Proof of Theorem \ref{thm:4}} We start with the following setup : \[\begin{tikzcd} \iota A \arrow[d, "\iota a"'] \\ \iota \Omega \arrow[rr, "F"'] & & \iota \Omega' \arrow[rr, "F'"'] & & \iota \Omega'' & \end{tikzcd}\] This contains an object $A\in \Comma{\calX}{\Omega}$, and two composable arrows $F, F' \in \Comma{\iota}{\iota}$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix a slice object and two composable arrows.

nodes.name: Apply tau_F and tau_F' in succession
nodes.statement: We can apply the functors $\tau_F$ and $\tau_{F'}$ in succession to get \[\begin{tikzcd} \iota A \arrow[d, "\iota a"'] \arrow[rr, "\tau_{F} (a)"] & & \iota B \arrow[d, "\iota b"] \arrow[rr, "\tau_{F'} (b)"] & & \iota C \arrow[d, "\iota c"'] & \\ \iota \Omega \arrow[rr, "F"'] & & \iota \Omega' \arrow[rr, "F'"'] & & \iota \Omega'' & \end{tikzcd}\]
nodes.statement_short: Apply the induced functors one after the other.

nodes.name: Reduce to comparing composites
nodes.statement: To prove Theorem \ref{thm:4}, it has to be shown that the composition along the arrows in the upper row equals $\tau_{F'\circ F}$.
nodes.statement_short: Must show the composite equals $\tau_{F'\circ F}$.

nodes.name: Connecting morphism phi by minimality
nodes.statement: The object $\tau_{F'\circ F}(a)$ itself can be drawn as shown below : \[\begin{tikzcd} & & & & & \iota D \arrow[ldd, "\iota d", bend left] \arrow[ld, "! \iota \phi"'] \\ \iota A \arrow[d, "\iota a"'] \arrow[rr, "\tau_{F} (a)"] \arrow[rrrrru, "\tau_{F'\circ F} (a)", bend left] & & \iota B \arrow[d, "\iota b"] \arrow[rr, "\tau_{F'} (b)"] & & \iota C \arrow[d, "\iota c"'] & \\ \iota \Omega \arrow[rr, "F"'] & & \iota \Omega' \arrow[rr, "F'"'] & & \iota \Omega'' & \end{tikzcd}\] The connecting morphism $\phi : D \to C$ exists by the minimality of $\tau_{F'\circ F}(a)$. The upper commuting loop can be expressed as \[ \tau_{F'} (b) \circ \tau_{F} (a) = \iota \phi \circ \tau_{F'\circ F} (a) . \]
nodes.statement_short: Minimality of $\tau_{F'\circ F}(a)$ gives $\phi$ with the stated loop.

nodes.name: All three morphisms are surjective
nodes.statement: By Theorem \ref{thm:3}, all the three morphisms $\tau_{F} (a)$, $\tau_{F'} (b)$ and $\tau_{F'\circ F} (a)$ are surjective.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Theorem thm:3.

nodes.name: iota phi is surjective
nodes.statement: Thus by Lemma \ref{lem:surj_right_cancel}, $\iota \phi$ must be surjective too.
nodes.statement_short: Right cancellation (Lemma lem:surj_right_cancel).

nodes.name: iota phi is an isomorphism
nodes.statement: By Assumption \ref{A:4} $\iota \phi$ is also injective. Thus by Assumption \ref{A:5}, $\iota \phi$ is an isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Assumptions A:4 and A:5 make $\iota\phi$ an isomorphism.

nodes.name: Conclude functoriality up to iso
nodes.statement: This implies that $\tau_{F'} (b) \circ \tau_{F} (a)$ and $\tau_{F'\circ F} (a)$ are equal up to isomorphism. This completes the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:4}. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Composite equals $\tau_{F'\circ F}(a)$ up to isomorphism.

nodes.name: Objects correspond
nodes.statement: Since $\iota$ is assumed to be injective on objects, the objects of $\iota(\calX)$ are in bijection with the object of $\calX$. Thus each object in $\iota(\calX)$ corresponds to a unique image $\iota \Omega$, for some $\Omega \in ob(\calX)$.
nodes.statement_short: Injectivity on objects identifies objects of $\iota(\calX)$ with those of $\calX$.

nodes.name: Functoriality from Theorem thm:4
nodes.statement: The functoriality now follows from Theorem \ref{thm:4}. This completes the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:0}. \qed

nodes.statement: Since $\paran{ \Forget_1 }^{(R)}$ is a right inverse of $\Forget_1$ by Lemma \ref{lem:RIRA}, it only remains to be shown that there is a natural transformation $\paran{ \Forget_2 }^{(L)} \circ \Forget_2 \Rightarrow \Id_{\Comma{P}{Q}}$, called the \emph{counit}.

nodes.name: Trace the composite functor
nodes.statement: The diagram on the left below traces the action of this composite functor on an object $F$ (blue) of $\Comma{P}{Q}$ into an object (green) of $\Comma{P}{Q}$ : \[\begin{tikzcd} Pp \arrow[d, "F"', Akashi] \\ Qq \end{tikzcd} \;\begin{tikzcd} {} \arrow[rr, mapsto, "\Forget_2"] && {} \end{tikzcd} \; q \;\begin{tikzcd} {} \arrow[rr, mapsto, "\paran{ \Forget_2 }^{(L)}"] && {} \end{tikzcd} \; \begin{tikzcd} P 0_{\calP} = 0_{\calR} \arrow[d, "!_{Qq}", Shobuj] \\ Qq \end{tikzcd} ; \quad \begin{tikzcd} P0_{\calP} \arrow[d, "P(!_p)"', Holud] \arrow[r, "!_{Qq}", Shobuj] & Qq \arrow[d, "Q \Id_q", Holud]\\ Pp \arrow[r, "F", Akashi] & Qq \end{tikzcd}\] The diagram on the left demonstrates a commutation arising out of the initial element preserving property.

nodes.name: Counit components
nodes.statement: The descending yellow morphisms together constitute the connecting morphism of the counit transformation we seek. This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: The yellow morphisms give the counit.

nodes.name: Reduce via Lemma lem:RIRA
nodes.statement: The functor $\Forget_{1}^{(L)}$ is clearly a right inverse of $\Forget_{1}$. Thus again by Lemma \ref{lem:RIRA} , it is enough to show the existence of a natural transformation as shown on the left below : \[ \eta : \Forget_1^{(L)} \circ \Forget_1 \Rightarrow \Id , \quad \begin{tikzcd} \alpha a \arrow[d, "F"', Akashi] \\ \beta b \end{tikzcd}, \, \begin{tikzcd} b \arrow[d, "\phi"', Akashi] \\ b' \end{tikzcd} , \; \begin{tikzcd} {} \arrow[rr, "\eta", mapsto] && {} \end{tikzcd} \; \begin{tikzcd} & \alpha a \arrow[r, "F", Holud] \arrow[ld, "="] & \beta b \arrow[ld, "="'] \arrow[d, "\beta \Id_b", Holud] & \\ \alpha a \arrow[r, "F"', Akashi] & \beta b \arrow[d, "\phi"', Akashi] & \beta b \arrow[ld, "\phi"] & \\ & \beta b' & & \end{tikzcd}\]

Thus the conclusions of \eqref{eqn:T_T2_T3} along with \eqref{eqn:0lkd0e} hold and we get : \begin{equation} \begin{tikzcd} [row sep = large] \ArrowCat{ \Comma{\alpha}{\beta} } \arrow[dd, "DL"'] \arrow[rr, "UR", Shobuj] \arrow[bend left = 30, Holud, "\Forget_1", rrrr] && \UR{\alpha}{\beta}{\calB} \arrow[drrrr, "\Forget_2"'] \arrow[rr, "\Forget_1"] && \Comma{\alpha}{\beta} \arrow[drr, "\Forget_2"] \\ && && && \calB \\ \DL{\alpha}{\beta}{\calA} \arrow[rrrr, bend right=20, Holud, dotted, "\gamma_F"'] \arrow[ddrr, "\Forget_2"', bend right=20] \arrow[rr, "\bar{\gamma}_F"', Shobuj, dotted] && \UR{\alpha}{\beta}{\calB} \arrow[rr, "\Forget_1"] \arrow[urrrr, "\Forget_2"] && \Comma{\alpha}{\beta} \arrow[urr, "\Forget_2"'] \\ \\ && \Comma{\alpha}{\beta} \arrow[uuurrrr, "\Forget_2"', bend right=20] & \Comma{\Forget_2^{ \Comma{\alpha}{\beta}}}{b} \arrow[dr, Akashi, "\text{Restrict}"] \arrow[luu, Akashi, "\subseteq"] \\ \Comma{\calA}{a} \arrow[Akashi, rrru, bend right=40, "\bar{\tau}_F"'] \arrow[rrrr, bend right=30, Shobuj, "\Dyn_F"'] \arrow[Itranga]{uuu}{ \MapC{F} } \arrow[rr] && \star \arrow[u, Itranga, "F"] \arrow[uuuurrrr, Itranga, "b"', bend right=30] && \Comma{\calB}{b} \arrow[uuuurr, "\Forget_2"', bend right=30] \end{tikzcd} \end{equation}

nodes.name: Conclude both theorems
nodes.statement: The commutations in \eqref{eqn:thm:2} are included within the commutation of \eqref{eqn:nc0s3}. The claim of minimality in Theorem \ref{thm:1} follows from the construction of $\gamma_F$ as a limit. The commutation diagram in \eqref{eqn:BarTau_b} links this minimal comma object to minimal commutation squares completing $\begin{tikzcd} \alpha a' \arrow[d, "\alpha f"'] \\ \alpha a \arrow[r, "F"'] & \beta b \end{tikzcd}$. This completes the proof of Theorems \ref{thm:1} and \ref{thm:2}. \qed
